785.title: The pledge of Ridwan
785.hook: Uthman goes into Mecca as envoy and won't circle the Ka'bah without the Prophet; a rumor says he's been killed, and they pledge under a tree, Salamah three times (48:18; Bukhari; Muslim)
785.howItsDone: Muslims honor the companions of the tree named in 48:18, and the pledge of Ridwan is taught as part of the story of Hudaybiyyah in sirah classes and in commentaries on Surah al-Fath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrims turned back: a kneeling camel, a dry well, and a closed door at Hudaybiyyah. Your line was: stopped at the edge. When a door closed, did you take a breath before you pushed? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

Someone has to go into Mecca and talk. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Umar says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sent Uthman ibn Affan, because no one was held in higher regard in Mecca than he was. So Uthman goes in alone, to explain that they've come as pilgrims, not to fight. Then he doesn't come back. Time passes, and a rumor runs through the camp at Hudaybiyyah: Uthman has been killed. Everything depends on what they do next. Today: the pledge of Ridwan.
screen: `UTHMAN GOES IN ALONE.` → `HE DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `A RUMOR: UTHMAN IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: First, a small detail about Uthman, from the early biographers. While he was in Mecca, the Meccans told him: you're here, so go around the Ka'bah if you want to. And he refused. He said he would not circle it until the Messenger of Allah did. The thing they had all walked so far for was in front of him, and he wouldn't take it alone. Meanwhile, back at the camp, the Prophet called the people to pledge. He sat beneath a tree, and they came, one by one, and put their hand in his. Salamah ibn al-Akwa, in Sahih Muslim, tells his own part. He pledged early, among the first. Later, in the middle of the crowd, the Prophet said: pledge, Salamah. I already did, he said. And again, said the Prophet. So he pledged a second time. Near the end, it happened once more. Salamah, won't you pledge? I pledged at the start and in the middle. And again. So he pledged a third time. The sources word the promise differently: Salamah says they pledged unto death; Jabir, also in Muslim, says they pledged not to flee. And for Uthman, who wasn't there, the Prophet held up his right hand and said this is Uthman's hand, and pledged for him. Surah al-Fath gives the moment two verses. One says that those who pledge to the Prophet pledge to Allah, and then, in Pickthall's words: "The Hand of Allah is above their hands." The other says Allah was well pleased with the believers when they pledged beneath the tree. From that verse the pledge takes its name: ridwan, good pleasure. Uthman turned out to be alive. But the pledge had already been made, and made again.
screen: `UTHMAN WON'T CIRCLE THE KA'BAH ALONE.` · `HANDS IN HIS HAND, UNDER A TREE.` · `AND AGAIN, SALAMAH.` · `THE HAND OF ALLAH IS ABOVE THEIR HANDS.` · then, large: `UNDER THE TREE.`

segments.voice: The practice: renew a pledge. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind a promise you made once and haven't said out loud in a long time: to a spouse, a friend, a child, to your own health, to your faith if you have one. You made it at the start. Now, somewhere in the middle, make it again, quietly, in your own words, the way Salamah did when he was told: and again. If you pray, you can renew it before Allah. If you don't, simply hold the promise in mind. Picture a tree and a hand. The bell holds the time.
Ridwan, good pleasure: the name of the pledge made beneath a tree at Hudaybiyyah, from surah 48:18, Allah was pleased with them. Today's word.
Your line: under the tree. Today, say one old promise again to the person you made it to, even if they never asked. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

786.title: The erased title
786.hook: the Meccan envoy objects to "Messenger of Allah" in the treaty; Ali won't erase it, so the Prophet ﷺ erases it himself (Bukhari; Muslim)
786.howItsDone: The treaty of Hudaybiyyah is taught in sirah classes and in commentaries on Surah al-Fath, and the erased title is retold as an example of the Prophet's patience in making peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pledge of Ridwan: hands under a tree, Uthman who wouldn't circle the Ka'bah alone, and Salamah told: and again. Your line was: under the tree. Did you say an old promise again? Day seven hundred eighty-six.

A treaty is being written at Hudaybiyyah. Ali ibn Abi Talib holds the pen. Across from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ sits Suhayl ibn Amr, sent by Mecca to make terms. Everyone around them is tense: they came as pilgrims, they've been turned back, a friend was feared dead. Now they're arguing about what to put on paper. And, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, Suhayl objects to the very first line. Today: the erased title.
screen: `A TREATY AT HUDAYBIYYAH.` → `ALI HOLDS THE PEN.` → `SUHAYL OBJECTS.`

segments.voice: The Prophet tells Ali to write: in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Suhayl says: the Beneficent, al-Rahman? I don't know what that is. Write: in Your name, O Allah, as you used to write. The Muslims want the full line. The Prophet says: write it his way. Next line: this is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed to. Suhayl stops him again. If we believed you were the Messenger of Allah, he says, we wouldn't have kept you from the House or fought you. Write: Muhammad, son of Abdullah. And the Prophet answers with something worth hearing twice: by Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah, even if you deny me. Write Muhammad, son of Abdullah. Then the moment the title is named for. In al-Bara's report, in Bukhari, the Prophet tells Ali to erase the words, Messenger of Allah, and Ali says: no, by Allah, I will never erase it. Some readers hear love in that, not stubbornness: he can't bring himself to rub out the title of the man he follows. Sahih Muslim adds the detail: the Prophet says, show me where it is. Ali shows him the place on the page. And the Prophet erases it with his own hand. Notice what he gave up, and what he didn't. He never stopped saying who he was. He said it out loud, to Suhayl's face. What he let go of was the word on the page. At the kneeling camel he had already said it: any plan that honors what Allah made sacred, he would grant. And notice Ali. The reports record no rebuke for his refusal. The Prophet simply did it himself.
screen: `IN YOUR NAME, O ALLAH.` · `I AM THE MESSENGER OF ALLAH, EVEN IF YOU DENY ME.` · `I WILL NEVER ERASE IT.` · `SHOW ME WHERE IT IS.` · then, large: `PEACE OVER PRIDE.`

segments.voice: The practice: give way on a word for peace. Sit, and settle your breath. Think of an argument you're in, at home, at work, or in a group chat, that's stuck on a word: an apology worded just so, a title, who said it first, whose name goes on top. Ask yourself the Prophet's question: am I giving up what's true, or only the wording? If the truth stays true either way, picture yourself taking the pen and erasing the word yourself. Notice whether anything loosens. If you pray, you can ask Allah for peace between you. If you don't, just hold the other person in mind, kindly. The bell holds the time.
Suhayl, the Meccan negotiator who objected to the treaty's first lines until the Prophet erased his own title rather than lose the peace. Today's word.
Your line: peace over pride. Today, let go of one word you've been holding out for, as long as the truth underneath it stays true. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

787.title: Umm Salamah's advice
787.hook: at Hudaybiyyah the upset companions won't move, until on Umm Salamah's advice he shaves his own head first
787.howItsDone: Muslims retell the Hudaybiyyah story from Sahih al-Bukhari, and Umm Salamah's counsel is cited when teachers speak of consultation (shura), including with one's family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prophet rubbed out his own title from the treaty so the peace could be signed. Your line was: peace over pride. Where did you give way on a word? Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

The treaty is signed. Nobody is celebrating. The companions came all this way in pilgrim white, and now they are going home without reaching the Ka'bah. The terms feel like a loss to them. So when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stands up and tells them to slaughter their sacrifice animals and shave their heads, the sign that the pilgrimage is over, nobody moves. He says it again. Still, no one stands. A leader, a crowd, and silence. Today: Umm Salamah's advice.
screen: `THE TREATY IS SIGNED.` → `SLAUGHTER AND SHAVE.` → `NOBODY MOVES.`

segments.voice: The long report in Sahih al-Bukhari tells what happens next. He goes into his tent, to his wife Umm Salamah, who has traveled with him, and tells her what the people have done. She doesn't scold them, and she doesn't tell him to give a speech. Her counsel is short and practical. Go out, she says. Don't say a word to anyone. Slaughter your own animal, and call your barber to shave your head. That's all. He does exactly that. He walks out, speaks to no one, slaughters his animal, and sits for the barber. And the moment they see it, the companions get up. They slaughter their animals and begin shaving one another's heads, the report says, so overcome with grief that they almost hurt one another. Some readers see it this way: the companions weren't defying him. They were grieving, and perhaps still hoping. As long as he hadn't shaved, maybe the plan would change. Words couldn't end that hope gently. His own shaved head could. Once he did it first, the question was closed, and they could follow. Notice also who saved the day. Not a general, not a famous speaker. A wife in a tent, asked for her opinion and taken at her word. Muslim teachers point to this scene when they talk about consulting family, and about how a hard instruction lands differently when the person giving it goes first.
screen: `HE TELLS UMM SALAMAH.` · `SAY NOTHING. SHAVE FIRST.` · `THEY RISE AND FOLLOW.` · `A WIFE'S COUNSEL, TAKEN.` · then, large: `DO IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: The practice: lead by doing it first. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one thing you keep asking other people to do. Tidy up, put the phone down, apologize, show up on time. Notice how often it's been words. Now picture yourself simply doing it, first, without announcing it. No speech. Just the act. Then think of one person whose advice you could ask today, the way he asked Umm Salamah. If you pray, you can ask Allah for the humility to go first. The bell holds the time.
Umm Salamah, the Prophet's wife whose quiet counsel, say nothing, and shave your own head first, ended the standoff at Hudaybiyyah. Today's word.
Your line: do it first. Today, pick one thing you've been asking for, and quietly do it yourself before you ask again. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

788.title: The emperor's questions
788.hook: Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, and Abu Sufyan can't bring himself to lie
788.carry: even his enemy told the truth
788.howItsDone: Muslims read the Heraclius report near the start of Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is retold as an account of the Prophet's character given by someone who was then his opponent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on Umm Salamah's advice, the Prophet said nothing and shaved his own head, and everyone followed. Your line was: do it first. What did you go first on? Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

A trade caravan from Mecca is doing business in Syria during the truce. Abu Sufyan, a leader of the Prophet's opponents in Mecca, is with it. Then a summons arrives. The Roman emperor, Heraclius, wants to question these Arabs, and asks which of them is the closest relative of the man who claims to be a prophet. Abu Sufyan is. So he finds himself in a royal court, with an interpreter, standing in front of an emperor. Behind him the emperor places his own companions, and tells them: if he lies to me, say so. Today: the emperor's questions.
screen: `A CARAVAN IN SYRIA.` → `SUMMONED TO THE EMPEROR.` → `IF HE LIES, SAY SO.`

segments.voice: This report sits in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on how revelation began, in Abu Sufyan's own telling. Heraclius asks about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, one plain question at a time. What is his family like among you? Has anyone among you made this claim before him? Do his followers come from the powerful, or the weak? Are they growing or shrinking? Does anyone leave his religion out of resentment? Did you ever accuse him of lying before he made this claim? Does he break his word? What does he tell you to do? And here's the line that makes the story. Abu Sufyan admits that if he hadn't been afraid of his companions reporting him as a liar, he would have lied. But they were right behind him. So he answered straight. He says the only place he could slip in a little doubt was this: we're in a truce with him now, and we don't know what he'll do in it. Then Heraclius goes back through every answer. A man who never lied about people, he reasons, would not start lying about God. The weak are the ones who follow messengers. Messengers don't betray. One answer after another, the enemy's own testimony draws a picture of an honest man. That's the strange gift in this story. Abu Sufyan didn't come to praise anyone. He came cornered, with his own companions at his back, and the truth came out of him anyway.
screen: `ONE PLAIN QUESTION AT A TIME.` · `HE WOULD HAVE LIED, BUT FOR SHAME.` · `ONE SMALL DOUBT SLIPPED IN.` · `THE ANSWERS DRAW AN HONEST MAN.` · then, large: `EVEN HIS ENEMY TOLD THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: answer truthfully about a rival. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Bring to mind someone you compete with, or simply don't like. A coworker, a sibling, an old friend you fell out with. Now ask yourself a few of the emperor's plain questions about them. Do they keep their word? Do they lie? Answer honestly, the way Abu Sufyan had to, with someone standing behind you. Notice where you'd like to slip in a little doubt. Let the honest answer stand. If you pray, you can ask Allah to keep your tongue truthful about the people you find hard. The bell holds the time.
Heraclius, the Roman emperor who questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, and whose own reasoning, drawn from an enemy's testimony, described an honest man. Today's word.
Your line: even his enemy told the truth. Today, when someone you find hard comes up in conversation, say only what's true about them, including the good. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

789.title: The oasis of Khaybar
789.hook: at the oasis of Khaybar, the flag is promised to a man nobody can guess, and given to Ali
789.howItsDone: Muslims retell the flag at Khaybar from Sahih al-Bukhari as a story about Ali ibn Abi Talib, and the Prophet's line that guiding one person is better than red camels is quoted in teaching about calling others gently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Sufyan stood before the emperor and couldn't bring himself to lie. Your line was: even his enemy told the truth. Did you say something true about a rival? Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

A camp outside the oasis of Khaybar, at night. The Muslim army is camped before its fortresses. Then the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, makes an announcement. Tomorrow, he says, I will give the flag to a man through whose hands Allah will grant victory, a man who loves Allah and His messenger, and whom Allah and His messenger love. And then he says nothing more. The report says the people spent the night talking it over, each one wondering: will it be me? Today: the oasis of Khaybar.
screen: `A CAMP AT KHAYBAR.` → `TOMORROW, THE FLAG.` → `WHO WILL IT BE?`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells the morning after. The companions come early, each hoping to be the one. And the Prophet asks a question no one expected: where is Ali ibn Abi Talib? They tell him Ali has a problem with his eyes. In other words, he's the one person who seems out of the running. The Prophet sends for him anyway. When Ali arrives, the Prophet applies his saliva to Ali's eyes and prays for him, and the report says Ali was healed as if he'd never had any pain. Then he hands him the flag. Look at Ali's first words. Not a celebration. A question: shall I fight them until they are like us? And the Prophet's answer slows him down. Go steadily, he tells him, until you reach their ground. Call them first, and tell them what is owed to Allah. Then he adds a line that is quoted to this day: that Allah should guide even one person through you is better for you than red camels. So the man nobody guessed, with sore eyes that morning, is given the task everyone had hoped for. And the first thing he's taught about it is patience. Khaybar is a hard chapter. It was home to Jewish communities, and the sirah tells of the fighting, the fall of the fortresses, and the agreement afterward that let its people keep farming the land. Today's lesson stays with one moment: a flag passing to someone who didn't look ready.
screen: `WHERE IS ALI?` · `HIS EYES ARE SORE.` · `HEALED, HANDED THE FLAG.` · `GO STEADILY. CALL THEM FIRST.` · then, large: `THE FLAG TO ALI.`

segments.voice: The practice: take on one hard task. Let your shoulders drop, and your breath lengthen. Bring to mind one hard thing you've been circling. A conversation, a form, a repair, an apology. Notice the reasons you're not ready. Tired, unsure, not the right person. Ali had a reason too. Now picture taking it on anyway, one small step, at a steady pace, the way he was told: go steadily. Choose the first step and hold it in mind. If you pray, you can ask Allah for strength in the task in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Khaybar, the oasis where the Prophet gave the flag to Ali, a man promised to be loved by Allah and His messenger. Today's word.
Your line: the flag to Ali. Today, take on the one hard task you've been putting off, and take the first step steadily, not in a rush. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

790.title: Sanctuary at Abu Sufyan's house
790.hook: entering Mecca, he declares safety for anyone in their own home, in the sacred mosque, or in Abu Sufyan's house
790.carry: whoever shuts his door is safe
790.howItsDone: Muslims retell the entry into Mecca from Sahih Muslim and the sirah, and the declaration of safety for Abu Sufyan's house and for anyone behind a closed door is told as a picture of mercy at the moment of victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, at the oasis of Khaybar, the flag went to Ali, whose eyes were sore that morning. Your line was: the flag to Ali. What hard task did you start? Day seven hundred ninety.

Mecca, the city that drove him out, is about to be entered by a large army. Inside, people are afraid of what the army will do to them. Now, a name we met two days ago: Abu Sufyan, the man who couldn't lie to the emperor. The sirah tells that he has just come over to the Muslim side, and he rides back into Mecca ahead of the army with a message from the Prophet. He stands in front of his own people and shouts what it is. Today: sanctuary at Abu Sufyan's house.
screen: `A CITY AFRAID.` → `ABU SUFYAN RIDES AHEAD.` → `A MESSAGE TO SHOUT.`

segments.voice: The message is about safety. Sahih Muslim records the words of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe. Whoever lays down his weapons is safe. Whoever shuts his door is safe. The sirah of Ibn Ishaq adds the sacred mosque around the Ka'bah as another place of safety. Look at how wide that is. You don't have to change your religion to be covered. You don't have to come out and surrender in public. You don't even have to leave your house. You only have to close your own front door, and you're protected. The safety comes to where people already are. And look at whose house is named. Not the house of an old friend. The house of Abu Sufyan, who had led the Meccans against the Muslims. Giving his home a share in the sanctuary is a kind of honor, and Abu Sufyan, of all people, is the one who announces it. A man who had been an enemy is handed a way to protect his own city. In the story, people go indoors and into the mosque. Muslims tell this as the day a city that had opposed him was entered with more mercy than it expected. Tomorrow we meet some of the people who had fought him hardest, and what happened when they came to him.
screen: `WHOEVER ENTERS ABU SUFYAN'S HOUSE.` · `WHOEVER LAYS DOWN WEAPONS.` · `SAFETY COMES TO WHERE PEOPLE ARE.` · `AN OLD ENEMY'S HOUSE, HONORED.` · then, large: `WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.`

segments.voice: The practice: make someone feel safe. Settle where you are, and let the breath slow. Think of a person who may be a little afraid of you. A child after you've raised your voice, a coworker who made a mistake, someone you argued with. Notice what they might be bracing for. Now picture the smallest step that would tell them: you're safe with me. Not a speech. A softer tone, a quick message, an easy word. Hold that step in mind. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make you a place of safety for others. The bell holds the time.
Abu Sufyan. The Prophet declared his house itself a sanctuary when Mecca was entered, safe for anyone who stayed inside or laid down weapons. Today's word.
Your line: whoever shuts his door is safe. Today, take that one small step toward the person who's bracing, and let them know they're safe with you. Day seven hundred ninety.

fork.reveal: whoever shuts his door is safe. safety came to where people already were.

original.note: Arabic: 'safe', the word repeated in each line of the declaration.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of safe places during a conquest.
what it means: safety offered so widely that closing your own door was enough, and an old enemy's house became a sanctuary.
what a scholar hears: the declaration in Sahih Muslim's book of jihad, with the sacred mosque added in Ibn Ishaq's sirah.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the conquest of Mecca)

791.title: The forgiven
791.hook: Hind, Ikrimah, Wahshi and others who fought him are forgiven when they come to him
791.howItsDone: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca from Sahih al-Bukhari and the sirah, and the stories of Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah are told as examples of the Prophet's mercy toward former enemies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Sufyan's house as sanctuary, and safety for anyone behind a closed door. Your line was: whoever shuts his door is safe. Who did you help feel safe? Day seven hundred ninety-one.

This week walked a long road. A pledge under a tree. A title rubbed out for peace. A wife's advice: do it first. An emperor's questions. A flag at Khaybar. A city of closed doors. And now, with Mecca entered, a harder question. What happens to the people who had hurt him badly? A man who killed the Prophet's uncle. A woman who celebrated that death. The son of a leading opponent. One by one, they come. Today: the forgiven.
screen: `A WEEK ON THE ROAD.` → `MECCA ENTERED.` → `WHAT ABOUT THE ONES WHO HURT HIM?`

segments.voice: Start with Wahshi. At Uhud he killed Hamza, the uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps Wahshi's own account. Later, he comes to the Prophet with a group from Ta'if, and accepts Islam. The Prophet asks: are you Wahshi? Are you the one who killed Hamza? Wahshi says it happened as he's heard. And the Prophet accepts him, and then asks one thing: can you keep your face away from me? That detail is honest. Forgiveness here doesn't mean the grief is gone. The door is open, and the wound is still a wound. Then Hind, Abu Sufyan's wife, who had stood against him at Uhud. Bukhari records what she said to him after she accepted Islam: once there was no household on earth she wanted more to see disgraced than his, and now there's none she wants more to see honored. Then Ikrimah, son of Abu Jahl, who fled Mecca toward Yemen to escape. The sirah tells that his wife, Umm Hakim, asked the Prophet for his safety, got it, and went after her husband to bring him home. He was received, not punished. Notice what these stories have in common. None of the three earns it by being useful first. Each one simply comes. And each one is met by a door that was already open. That doesn't erase what they did. The stories remember it plainly, right beside Hind's sentence about a household she now wanted to see honored.
screen: `WAHSHI: KEEP YOUR FACE AWAY.` · `HIND: NOW, HONORED.` · `IKRIMAH: BROUGHT HOME BY HIS WIFE.` · `EACH ONE SIMPLY COMES.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYED OPEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: forgive a real hurt. Sit still for a moment, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one real hurt, not the biggest one, one you can hold for two minutes. Let yourself remember it plainly, the way the stories remember Uhud. Then notice: forgiving doesn't require pretending it didn't hurt. The Prophet still asked Wahshi to keep his face away. You can keep a boundary and still open a door. Picture leaving that door unlocked, even a crack. If you pray, you can ask Allah to forgive them, and to forgive you. The bell holds the time.
The forgiven. Wahshi, Hind, Ikrimah and others who had fought the Prophet were accepted when they came to him, their past remembered but not held against them. Today's word.
Your line: the door stayed open. Today, leave one door open a crack for someone who hurt you. A boundary can stay. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

myth: forgiving Wahshi meant the Prophet acted as if nothing happened
he accepted him, and asked him to keep his face away.
Ikrimah's wife asked for his safety and brought him back
the sirah tells Umm Hakim went after him once his safety was granted.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. the man who killed your uncle stands in front of you and accepts Islam. what do you do?
options: refuse him.
accept him, and ask him to keep his face away from you.
accept him and say it never happened.
fork.reveal: he accepted Wahshi, and asked: can you keep your face away from me? the door was open, and the grief was honest.

original.note: Arabic: pardon, letting a wrong go; al-'Afuw, the Pardoner, is one of the names of Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone was forgiven, end of story.
what it means: forgiveness that remembers plainly, keeps an honest boundary, and still lets people come home.
what a scholar hears: Wahshi's own account of Hamza's death and his later acceptance of Islam, preserved in Bukhari's book of military campaigns.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3825 (Hind's words to the Prophet)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah; Malik, al-Muwatta, book of marriage (Ikrimah and Umm Hakim)
